title: Bravery and Courage

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: There are no true cowards, according to psychologist Robert Biswas-Diener of Portland State University. Instead, he claims, all people demonstrate different types of courage, to varying degrees. ‘Courage is a habit... a skill that can be learned,’ says Biswas-Diener. Mention courage and we might picture a dramatic scene like a hero rescuing a baby from a burning building – there would be universal acceptance that this constituted courage. But Biswas-Diener argues that courage is just as necessary for routine acts such as requesting a pay rise or meeting new friends. Clinical psychologist Cynthia Pury splits courage into two categories: ‘accolade courage’ for acts of no direct advantage to the person who shows it, such as rescuing a child, and ‘process courage,’ when the end goal is only of importance to the individual concerned, such as skydiving.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One interesting question concerns whether there’s a gender difference. Certainly, men have traditionally received far more awards for acts of physical bravery than women. But Biswas-Diener believes this could be because men are physically stronger and more likely to join the military or emergency services, where there is a greater likelihood they will be called on to display the sort of courage that wins medals. And he is adamant that women’s bravery simply manifests itself in different ways, pointing out that women donate 57% of kidneys in the US, and make up the majority of volunteers for good causes such as the Peace Corps – the sort of acts that go largely unnoticed. Pury argues that understanding courage requires that we understand something of an individual’s personality, so we can assess what fears they had to overcome and how much the goal mattered.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: So are heroes born or made? Genetics play a part, Pury explains, because some of us are born with less of a general fear response than others. But people can also consciously affect the process. Biswas-Diener thinks of courage as a see-saw going up and down in a child’s playground, with fear and risk at one end and a worthwhile goal at the other. To become more courageous, he says, we need to reduce the fear or risk, or give more weight to the goal. Fire department Chief Kerry Gregory recognizes something similar: saying his firefighters are trained to assess risk and, if necessary, withdraw from certain environments, however hard this decision may be. In a 2006 study, Pury surveyed 256 students about the times they showed courage, and found that 82% had deliberately taken actions to reduce their fear. Today, Debra Taylor-Hayhurst is an expert in speech-making, but she admits that, like many others, she used to be terrified of public speaking. So how did she change this? ‘Practice, practice, practice – just doing it,’ she says. She remembers driving home from practice sessions feeling absolutely elated that she’d managed to make a speech despite feeling terribly anxious.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Stage fright is apparently quite common even among professionals. Three years ago former news presenter Carol Hirschfeld revealed that she used to take a type of heart regulating drug called beta-blockers before going on screen to cope with massive performance anxiety. ‘That just calmed my heartbeat down, really. It was under doctor’s supervision. It helped to feel my heart wasn’t going to escape from my chest cavity while I was reading.’ Apparently, she’s far from alone; film-maker and writer Polly Morland cites a recent study of eight premier Australian orchestras, which found that almost one in three of the 357 musicians were taking beta-blockers to manage their performance anxiety.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The good news is that courage can be cumulative. ‘Cumulative courage’ is the idea that a single courageous act can increase a person’s bravery in other areas. For example, imagine a person goes through with a bungee jump despite a fear of heights. Pury would advise the person to immediately go out and buy themselves some souvenir to mark the occasion. Then, before driving to a big job interview say, take a moment to look at it and think, ‘I jumped off a bridge. I can do this.’ She also advises people to focus on the process of bravery, not the outcome. So it’s wrong if an action can only be termed as courageous if it results in success. It’s possible that an attempt to rescue someone might fail, but that doesn’t make the attempt any less brave, Pury argues. Biswas-Diener advises building up courage by taking on ‘brave roles’ to develop a sense of being able to control one’s own destiny. This might be something very little, like being prepared to sample a food never tasted before; numerous little steps might be more beneficial than one big one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other factors also contribute to cumulative courage. Psychologists cautiously recommend a rather surprising strategy: turn fear into anger, because this ‘puts our bodies on course to act quickly and strongly, often overriding our doubts,’ according to Biswas-Diener. And finally, there is an even more surprising suggestion. A 2010 German study published in Psychological Research found that those people who in some way harness the power of superstition did better when tested on tasks that measured bravery. Many people have these little beliefs, and they seem to boost self-confidence. It is just one more way in which individuals can cumulatively enhance their courage and bravery.
